note: The counted exception to fill-empty-only: every theme here exists in the source with a band-suffixed description (the documented content debt); this promotion replaces exactly those rows with five authored sentences per theme. The normaliser refuses any other target. Track names, prefixes, codes, credentials and transfer checks are untouched.

themes.theme: What a model is and is not
themes.description: What a language model is, mechanically, at the level that predicts its behaviour.

bands.K–2: Say in your own words that a chat helper guesses the next words from what it has read, and is not a person.
bands.3–5: Explain to a classmate how a language model predicts words, and one way that makes it get things wrong.
bands.6–8: Explain how a language model works to somebody else and have them predict a failure from your explanation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain it to somebody else and have them predict a failure from your explanation.
bands.11–12: Explain the mechanism to a real non-specialist audience and have them predict failures, then test their predictions live.

themes.theme: Training data, and where it came from
themes.description: Training data, its origins, and what that implies about what a model reflects.

bands.K–2: Say where a chat helper learned its words from, and whose words are missing.
bands.3–5: Find out what kinds of writing a model was trained on and name one kind it would not have seen.
bands.6–8: Identify what a given model was trained on from its documentation, and what that omits, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify what a given model was trained on, and what that omits.
bands.11–12: Identify the training data of a model in real use at an organisation, what it omits, and what that means for the people it serves.

themes.theme: Why a fluent answer can be wrong
themes.description: Fluency and accuracy are separate properties, and fluency is the one you perceive.

bands.K–2: Find an answer from a chat helper that sounds sure but is wrong, and say how you knew.
bands.3–5: Find a smooth, confident wrong answer and explain why it sounded right.
bands.6–8: Find a fluent wrong answer and explain why it reads as confident, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find a fluent wrong answer and explain why it reads as confident.
bands.11–12: Collect fluent wrong answers in a real domain, explain the fluency, and write the guidance a team would need.

themes.theme: Confidence, and why it is not accuracy
themes.description: Stated confidence is not calibrated probability, and treating it as one is the common error.

bands.K–2: Ask a chat helper five easy questions and check each answer with an adult.
bands.3–5: Collect five confident answers from a model and check each against a book.
bands.6–8: Collect five confident answers and check them against sources, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Collect five confident answers and check them.
bands.11–12: Collect confident answers in a real workflow, check them, and report the accuracy rate to the people relying on them.

themes.theme: Prompting as a skill
themes.description: Prompting as a skill with technique, limits, and diminishing returns.

bands.K–2: Ask a helper the same question two ways and say which got the better answer.
bands.3–5: Improve one answer from a model by changing how you asked, and write down what you changed.
bands.6–8: Improve one task's output measurably by prompting and document what changed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Improve one task's output measurably and document what changed.
bands.11–12: Improve a real task's output measurably, document the technique, and hand it to a team with its limits stated.

themes.theme: The same question, asked five ways
themes.description: Asking the same question five ways to see the variance the single answer hides.

bands.K–2: Ask a helper the same thing five different ways and notice whether the answers agree.
bands.3–5: Ask a model one question five ways and write down how much the answers differed.
bands.6–8: Run the five-ways experiment on one question and report the spread, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Run the experiment and report the spread.
bands.11–12: Run the experiment on a real question that matters to an organisation and report the spread to the people who use the single answer.

themes.theme: Checking an answer you cannot verify
themes.description: Checking an answer in a domain where you cannot judge it, which is the real problem.

bands.K–2: When a helper tells you something you cannot check, say who you would ask.
bands.3–5: Plan how to check a model's answer about something you know nothing about.
bands.6–8: Design a verification route for a domain outside your expertise, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a verification route for a domain outside your expertise.
bands.11–12: Design and use a verification route for a real domain outside your expertise, and record where it failed.

themes.theme: Hallucination as a property, not a bug
themes.description: Fabrication as a property of the mechanism rather than a defect to be patched out.

bands.K–2: Say why a helper sometimes makes things up, using the word-guessing idea.
bands.3–5: Explain why a model invents facts, from how it works, not as a mistake somebody forgot to fix.
bands.6–8: Explain why fabrication happens, from the mechanism, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain why it happens, from the mechanism.
bands.11–12: Explain fabrication from the mechanism to a real team and turn the explanation into a rule for when they may rely on the output.

themes.theme: What a model cannot know about you
themes.description: What a model cannot know about you, and the inferences it will make anyway.

bands.K–2: Say what a chat helper knows about you: only what you typed.
bands.3–5: List what a model actually has about you and what it is guessing.
bands.6–8: List what a model actually has and what it is inferring in one real interaction, with a checker.
bands.9–10: List what it actually has and what it is inferring.
bands.11–12: Audit a real deployed assistant for what it has about a user and what it infers, and write the notice the user is owed.

themes.theme: Reading a model card
themes.description: Reading a model card for the limitations rather than the benchmarks.

bands.K–2: With an adult, find the part of a helper's description that says what it cannot do.
bands.3–5: Read a model's information page and write two things it says it is bad at.
bands.6–8: Read one model card and state three limitations in your own words, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read one and state three limitations in your own words.
bands.11–12: Read the model card for a system in real use and state the limitations that apply to that use, for the people using it.

tracks.name: Using one at work or school

themes.theme: The task it is good at
themes.description: Identifying the tasks where assistance genuinely helps, from evidence rather than habit.

bands.K–2: Try a class task with a helper and without, and say which was better and why.
bands.3–5: Test one school task with and without a model and measure the difference.
bands.6–8: Test one task both ways and measure the difference, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Test one task both ways and measure the difference.
bands.11–12: Test a real work task both ways with measured criteria and report the difference to the team.

themes.theme: The task it is bad at
themes.description: The tasks where it degrades the work, including ones where the degradation is invisible.

bands.K–2: Find a task a helper does badly and say how you would notice.
bands.3–5: Find a school task a model makes worse and say how nobody would notice.
bands.6–8: Find one task a model degrades and describe how the failure would be missed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find one and describe how the failure would be missed.
bands.11–12: Find a real task a model degrades invisibly and put the finding to the people who rely on it.

themes.theme: Disclosure: saying you used one
themes.description: Disclosure: when to say you used one, to whom, and in what form.

bands.K–2: When a helper helped with your work, say so on the work.
bands.3–5: Write a note on a piece of school work saying what a model did and what you did.
bands.6–8: Write a disclosure statement for one real piece of work, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a disclosure statement for one real piece of work.
bands.11–12: Write and attach disclosure statements for real work over a month, and agree the form with the people who receive it.

themes.theme: Your own work versus assisted work
themes.description: The line between your work and assisted work, drawn by you before somebody draws it for you.

bands.K–2: Say which parts of a drawing or story were yours and which a helper did.
bands.3–5: Draw your own line between your work and a model's help, and explain it to a teacher.
bands.6–8: Define your own line between your work and assisted work and defend it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Define your own line between your work and assisted work, and defend it to somebody who assesses you.
bands.11–12: Define the line for a real team and get it adopted before somebody else draws it for you.

themes.theme: Where the output goes
themes.description: Where the output goes, who retains it, and what that means for what you paste in.

bands.K–2: Say where your words go when you type them into a helper, and who might keep them.
bands.3–5: Read what a service keeps of what you type and say what you can no longer control.
bands.6–8: Read one service's retention terms and state what leaves your control, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read one service's retention terms and state what leaves your control.
bands.11–12: Read the retention terms of a service a real organisation uses and write the guidance on what may be pasted in.

themes.theme: Confidential information and the box
themes.description: Confidential information and the box: the rule, and the reason people break it.

bands.K–2: Say what you should never type into a helper: passwords, addresses, other people's secrets.
bands.3–5: List what school information you may not paste into a model, and why people do it anyway.
bands.6–8: Identify what you may not paste into a model and the pressure that would make you, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify what you may not paste, and the pressure that would make you.
bands.11–12: Identify the rule for a real organisation, the pressure that breaks it, and one control that relieves the pressure.

themes.theme: A model in a hiring decision
themes.description: A model in a hiring decision, and what a candidate is owed.

bands.K–2: Say whether a computer should decide who gets a job, and what the person should be told.
bands.3–5: Say what someone applying for a job should be told if a model reads their application.
bands.6–8: State what an applicant should be told and the recourse they should have, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State what an applicant should be told, and the recourse they should have.
bands.11–12: State what applicants are owed for a real hiring process and check it against what they are actually told.

themes.theme: A model marking your work
themes.description: A model marking your work, and the appeal route that should exist.

bands.K–2: Say what you would want to happen if a computer marked your work wrong.
bands.3–5: Design how you would appeal a mark a model gave you.
bands.6–8: Design the appeal route you would want for model-marked work, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design the appeal route you would want when a model has marked your work.
bands.11–12: Design the appeal route for a real setting where a model marks work, and get it adopted.

themes.theme: Refusing to use one
themes.description: Refusing to use one, and making the refusal legible rather than merely stubborn.

bands.K–2: Say why you might choose to do a task without a helper, in a way a teacher could accept.
bands.3–5: Write why you will not use a model for one school task, so somebody could act on it.
bands.6–8: Write a refusal to use a model in terms somebody could act on, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the refusal in terms somebody could act on.
bands.11–12: Write and deliver a real refusal to a real manager or teacher in actionable terms, and record the response.

themes.theme: Keeping the skill you delegated
themes.description: Keeping a skill you have delegated, which requires deliberately not delegating it sometimes.

bands.K–2: Do a task by hand this week that you usually let a helper do, and say what you noticed.
bands.3–5: Plan when you will do a task yourself even though a model could, so you keep the skill.
bands.6–8: Design a practice schedule for one delegated skill, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a practice schedule for one delegated skill.
bands.11–12: Design and follow a practice schedule for a real delegated skill for a term, and measure whether it held.

themes.theme: Bias that is measurable
themes.description: Bias you can measure, the metrics that exist, and what each metric misses.

bands.K–2: Ask a helper to draw or describe ten people and count who is missing.
bands.3–5: Test a model's outputs for one kind of unfairness you can count, and say what counting misses.
bands.6–8: Apply one fairness metric to a real output set and state its blind spot, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Apply one fairness metric to a real output set and state its blind spot.
bands.11–12: Apply fairness metrics to a system in real use, state their blind spots, and report to the people accountable for it.

themes.theme: Bias that is not
themes.description: Bias you cannot measure, which is most of it, and reasoning about it anyway.

bands.K–2: Say one unfair thing a helper might do that would be hard to count.
bands.3–5: Find one unfairness in a system that you cannot measure and say which way it probably goes.
bands.6–8: Identify one unmeasurable bias in a real system and argue its likely direction, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one unmeasurable bias in a real system and argue its likely direction.
bands.11–12: Identify unmeasurable biases in a system in real use, argue their direction, and write them into its documentation.

themes.theme: Automation of a decision about a person
themes.description: Automating a decision about a person, and the threshold at which that becomes unacceptable.

bands.K–2: Say one decision about a person that a computer should never make alone.
bands.3–5: Take one decision about a person and say where a computer should stop and a person decide.
bands.6–8: Take one decision and argue where the line for automation sits, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Take one decision and argue where the line sits.
bands.11–12: Argue the line for a real automated decision to the people who run it, and record what they decided.

themes.theme: Surveillance dressed as a service
themes.description: Services whose value proposition is surveillance, recognised from the design.

bands.K–2: Find an app that watches you to be helpful, and say what it watches.
bands.3–5: Find one product that is convenient because it watches you, and say what it collects.
bands.6–8: Identify the surveillance in one product presented as convenience, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify the surveillance in one product presented as convenience.
bands.11–12: Identify the surveillance in a product a real organisation uses and write what its users should be told.

themes.theme: Deepfakes and the person in them
themes.description: Synthetic media of a real person, and what that person is owed.

bands.K–2: Say why making a fake picture of a real person is wrong, and what they could do about it.
bands.3–5: Say what a person in a fake video is owed and who could help them.
bands.6–8: State the obligations to a person in synthetic media, and the recourse that currently exists, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State the obligations, and the recourse that currently exists.
bands.11–12: State the obligations and the real recourse where you live, and test the recourse with a real or worked case.

themes.theme: Persuasion and the warm voice
themes.description: Persuasion delivered warmly, and why warmth defeats scepticism.

bands.K–2: Notice when a helper sounds friendly and say why that makes you believe it more.
bands.3–5: Look at one friendly message from a system and find how the friendliness persuades.
bands.6–8: Analyse one persuasive interaction and identify the mechanism, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Analyse one persuasive interaction and identify the mechanism.
bands.11–12: Analyse persuasive interactions in a real product and write the guidance its users need to resist them.

themes.theme: Dependency and what it costs
themes.description: Dependency and what it costs, including the capabilities that quietly stop being practised.

bands.K–2: Say one thing you can do less well because a device does it for you.
bands.3–5: Audit what you rely on one app for and what you would lose without it.
bands.6–8: Audit your own dependence on one system and what you would lose, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Audit your own dependence on one system and what you would lose.
bands.11–12: Audit a real team's dependence on one system and what it would lose, and plan the practice that keeps the skill.

themes.theme: Children and systems that reason
themes.description: Children interacting with systems that reason, and the protections that do not yet exist.

bands.K–2: Say what a chat helper should never do with a child, and who should make the rules.
bands.3–5: State what protection a child using a chat system should have, and why it is missing.
bands.6–8: State what protection you would require for children and why the current position fails it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State what protection you would require, and why the current position fails it.
bands.11–12: State the protection you would require for a real setting with children, compare it with what exists, and put the gap to the people responsible.

themes.theme: Work that disappears
themes.description: Work that disappears, described by the people whose work it was.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult about a job that a machine now does, and listen without arguing.
bands.3–5: Find one account by a person whose work a system replaced and retell it faithfully.
bands.6–8: Find one account of work that disappeared and present it without softening, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find one account and present it without softening.
bands.11–12: Collect accounts of work that disappeared in a real sector and present them unsoftened to the people deploying the systems.

themes.theme: Concentration of who owns the systems
themes.description: Concentration of ownership, and why it is a governance question rather than a market one.

bands.K–2: Say how many companies make the helpers people use, and why that matters.
bands.3–5: Find out who owns the systems in one area and what that lets them decide.
bands.6–8: Map who controls the systems in one domain and what that permits, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map who controls the systems in one domain and what that permits.
bands.11–12: Map control of the systems in a real domain and present what it permits to a body that governs it.

themes.theme: Who decides what a system may do
themes.description: Who actually decides what a system may do, traced to named accountable people.

bands.K–2: Say who decides what a class computer is allowed to do, by name.
bands.3–5: Trace who decides what one school system may do, to a named person.
bands.6–8: Trace one real system to a named decision-maker, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace one real system to a named decision-maker.
bands.11–12: Trace a system in real use to its named accountable people and confirm with them that they hold the decision.

themes.theme: A gate, and why it is a person
themes.description: A gate is a person because accountability requires somebody who can be asked and answer.

bands.K–2: Say why there should be a person you can ask when a computer says no.
bands.3–5: Find the person behind one rule a system enforces at school, or say there is none.
bands.6–8: Identify a gate in a real system and the person behind it, or its absence, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify a gate in a real system and the person behind it, or its absence.
bands.11–12: Identify the gates in a real deployment, name the person behind each, and report the ones with nobody.

themes.theme: Auditing something you cannot see inside
themes.description: Auditing a system you cannot inspect, and the techniques that work from outside.

bands.K–2: Work out what a black box does by trying things and watching, and say what you still cannot tell.
bands.3–5: Test a system from the outside to find one thing it does, and say what testing cannot show.
bands.6–8: Design an external audit for a system you have no access to, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design an external audit for a system you have no access to.
bands.11–12: Design and run an external audit of a real system you cannot inspect, and publish the method with the findings.

themes.theme: Regulation and its lag
themes.description: Regulatory lag, why it exists, and what fills the gap in the interval.

bands.K–2: Say why rules for new things arrive after the things do.
bands.3–5: Find one new technology with no rules yet and say what fills the gap.
bands.6–8: Identify one regulatory gap and what is currently filling it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one gap and what is currently filling it.
bands.11–12: Identify a real regulatory gap affecting a real organisation and write the interim policy it should adopt.

themes.theme: An impact assessment worth reading
themes.description: An impact assessment that would change a decision, versus one that documents a decision.

bands.K–2: Before doing something big in class, write what might go wrong for whom, and let it change the plan.
bands.3–5: Read a short assessment of a project's effects and say whether it could have changed the decision.
bands.6–8: Read one impact assessment and state whether it could have changed anything, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read one and state whether it could have changed anything.
bands.11–12: Read a real impact assessment for a real deployment, state whether it could have changed anything, and write the one that could.

themes.theme: Redress when a system is wrong
themes.description: Redress when a system is wrong: the route, its cost, and who can actually use it.

bands.K–2: Say what you would do if a computer got something about you wrong, and who would fix it.
bands.3–5: Map how somebody would get a wrong system decision fixed, and what it would cost them.
bands.6–8: Map a real redress route and identify who is excluded by its cost, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map a real redress route and identify who is excluded by its cost.
bands.11–12: Map the redress route for a system in real use, test it with a real or worked case, and report who it excludes.

themes.theme: Open weights and the argument about them
themes.description: Open weights: the strongest argument on each side, stated by somebody who holds neither.

bands.K–2: Say one good and one bad thing about giving everyone a powerful tool.
bands.3–5: State the best reason for sharing a model openly and the best reason against, fairly.
bands.6–8: Present both cases on open weights to a standard each side would accept, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Present both cases to a standard each side would accept.
bands.11–12: Present both cases to a real audience holding both views, and have each side confirm their case was stated fairly.

themes.theme: Compute, energy and water
themes.description: Compute, energy and water as physical inputs with locations and local consequences.

bands.K–2: Say that a helper runs on big computers that use electricity and water, and where they might be.
bands.3–5: Find where one data centre is and what it uses from the place around it.
bands.6–8: Locate one data centre and identify its local resource impact, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Locate one data centre and identify its local resource impact.
bands.11–12: Locate the data centres behind a real deployment, identify their local impacts, and include them in the deployment's accounting.

themes.theme: International agreement and its limits
themes.description: International agreement, what it can bind, and where it stops.

bands.K–2: Say what countries can agree together about new machines, and what they cannot make each other do.
bands.3–5: Find one agreement between countries about technology and say who enforces it.
bands.6–8: Identify one international agreement and the enforcement it actually has, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one agreement and the enforcement it actually has.
bands.11–12: Identify the agreements that touch a real deployment and what each actually binds, for the people accountable for it.

themes.theme: The refusal that is written down
themes.description: A refusal written down, versioned, and repealable only in public.

bands.K–2: Write one thing your class will never let a helper do, and say how the rule could be changed in public.
bands.3–5: Write one refusal for a school system and the way it could be changed openly.
bands.6–8: Write one refusal and the procedure by which it could be repealed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write one refusal and the procedure by which it could be repealed.
bands.11–12: Write a real refusal for a real organisation, versioned, with its public repeal procedure, and get it adopted.

themes.theme: Work, and what it is for
themes.description: Work and what it is for, asked before asking what should be automated.

bands.K–2: Say why people work, beyond money, and ask three adults the same.
bands.3–5: Write your own answer to what work is for and compare it with three people's.
bands.6–8: Write your own answer to what work is for and test it against three people's, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write your own answer and test it against three people's.
bands.11–12: Write your answer, test it against three people from different work, and publish the comparison.

themes.theme: Education after the answer is free
themes.description: What education is for once retrieval is free, which was always the real question.

bands.K–2: Say what school is for when a helper can answer any question.
bands.3–5: Argue what should be taught now that answers are easy to get.
bands.6–8: Argue what should be taught that was not being taught before, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Argue what should be taught that was not being taught before.
bands.11–12: Argue it to a real audience of educators and record what they would change.

themes.theme: What only people can do
themes.description: What only people can do, argued carefully rather than asserted comfortably.

bands.K–2: Say one thing only a person can do, and let a friend argue against it.
bands.3–5: Make the case for something only people can do and have a classmate attack it.
bands.6–8: Make the argument for what only people can do and have somebody attack it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Make the argument and have somebody attack it.
bands.11–12: Make the argument in public, have it attacked by somebody who disagrees, and revise it on the record.

themes.theme: Care as the durable economy
themes.description: Care as the economy that does not automate away, and what that implies about its pay.

bands.K–2: Say why looking after people is work a machine cannot take over, and whether it is paid enough.
bands.3–5: Follow the idea that caring work will remain to what it means for how carers are paid.
bands.6–8: Follow the argument about care work to its conclusion about wages, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Follow the argument to its conclusion about wages.
bands.11–12: Follow the argument to wages for a real care sector and present the conclusion to people who set them.

themes.theme: Deciding what not to build
themes.description: Deciding not to build something, and the institutional conditions that allow that decision.

bands.K–2: Say one thing people decided not to make, and why.
bands.3–5: Find one thing that was deliberately not built and say what let people decide that.
bands.6–8: Identify one thing that was not built and why, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one thing that was not built, and why.
bands.11–12: Identify a real case of deciding not to build, and the institutional conditions that allowed it, for a body facing the same decision.

themes.theme: A technology that arrived before its rules
themes.description: A technology arriving before its rules, and what happens in the interval.

bands.K–2: Find one old invention that arrived before the rules for it, and what happened first.
bands.3–5: Find a historical technology that came before its rules and say what the gap cost.
bands.6–8: Find a historical parallel and state what the interval cost, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find a historical parallel and state what the interval cost.
bands.11–12: Find the parallel, state the cost, and apply the lesson to a real technology in its interval now.

themes.theme: Being a citizen of a technical society
themes.description: Citizenship in a society whose infrastructure you cannot inspect.

bands.K–2: Say what you would need to know to understand the machines around you.
bands.3–5: List what a person needs to understand to be a good citizen when machines they cannot see make decisions.
bands.6–8: Identify what you would need to be a competent citizen in a technical society, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify what you would need to be a competent citizen here.
bands.11–12: Identify what competent citizenship requires here and design the education that would provide it.

themes.theme: Explaining this to somebody older
themes.description: Explaining this to somebody older, without condescension and without overclaiming.

bands.K–2: Explain to a grandparent what a chat helper is, and let them say if it made sense.
bands.3–5: Explain a model to somebody older without talking down, and be marked by them.
bands.6–8: Explain this to somebody older, without condescension or overclaiming, and be assessed by them.
bands.9–10: Explain this to somebody older, without condescension or overclaiming, and be assessed by them on both.
bands.11–12: Explain it to older people in a real setting and be assessed by them, then revise the explanation.

themes.theme: Explaining it to somebody younger
themes.description: Explaining it to somebody younger, who will live with the consequences longer.

bands.K–2: Explain to a younger child what a helper can and cannot do, and ask what they understood.
bands.3–5: Explain a model to a younger pupil who will live with it longer, and be marked by them.
bands.6–8: Explain this to somebody younger and be assessed by them, with a checker present.
bands.9–10: Explain this to somebody younger, who will live with the consequences longer, and be assessed by them.
bands.11–12: Explain it to younger people in a real setting, be assessed by them, and record what they asked that you had not thought of.

themes.theme: The world you would choose
themes.description: The world you would choose, written down, because a preference not stated is not a preference.

bands.K–2: Draw or write the world you would like machines to help make, clearly enough that a friend could disagree.
bands.3–5: Write the future you would choose specifically enough for a classmate to argue with.
bands.6–8: Write the world you would choose, specifically enough to be disagreed with, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write it, specifically enough to be disagreed with.
bands.11–12: Write it, publish it, and hold a real discussion with people who disagree.

themes.theme: Deciding whether a model belongs here at all
themes.description: The prior question, asked before design.

bands.K–2: Say one class job that should not use a helper, and why.
bands.3–5: Argue one case where a school should not use a model at all.
bands.6–8: Argue one case for not using a model in a described system, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Argue one case for not using a model at all in a system that was going to have one.
bands.11–12: Argue the case for a real proposed system to the people who want it, and record the decision.

themes.theme: What the system does when the model is wrong
themes.description: Designing for the error rather than the success case.

bands.K–2: Say what should happen when a helper gives a wrong answer in a game.
bands.3–5: Design what a school tool does when its model is wrong.
bands.6–8: Specify the failure behaviour for one described system, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Specify the failure behaviour for one system.
bands.11–12: Specify and test the failure behaviour of a real system before it is deployed.

themes.theme: A human in the loop, meaningfully
themes.description: The difference between review and rubber-stamping.

bands.K–2: Say the difference between really checking and just pressing OK.
bands.3–5: Design a checking step a person could actually use to change a result.
bands.6–8: Design a review step that could realistically change an outcome, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a review step that could realistically change an outcome.
bands.11–12: Design the review step for a real system and measure how often it changes an outcome.

themes.theme: Evaluation before deployment
themes.description: Testing against the cases that matter rather than the cases that are easy.

bands.K–2: Test a helper on the hard questions, not just the easy ones, before trusting it.
bands.3–5: Build a set of hard test questions for a school tool before using it.
bands.6–8: Build an evaluation set including hard cases for a described system, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build an evaluation set including hard cases.
bands.11–12: Build and run an evaluation set with hard cases for a real system, and report the failures before launch.

themes.theme: The data you are allowed to use
themes.description: Provenance, licence and consent for training or retrieval.

bands.K–2: Say whether you are allowed to use someone's story in a project, and how you would ask.
bands.3–5: Check one data source for where it came from and whether you may use it.
bands.6–8: Audit one data source for provenance, licence and consent, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Audit one data source for provenance, licence and consent before using it.
bands.11–12: Audit every data source of a real system for all three and stop the ones that fail.

themes.theme: Cost per interaction
themes.description: What a system costs to run, and who pays as it scales.

bands.K–2: Say that every question to a helper costs money and energy, and guess how much for a class.
bands.3–5: Work out what one school tool costs per use and at a hundred uses.
bands.6–8: Cost one described system at three volumes, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Cost one system per interaction at three volumes and say who pays as it scales.
bands.11–12: Cost a real system at three volumes and present who pays as it scales.

themes.theme: Monitoring after launch
themes.description: Drift, and the measurement that detects it.

bands.K–2: Say how you would notice if a helper started getting worse over time.
bands.3–5: Decide what to watch to know a school tool is drifting, and when to raise the alarm.
bands.6–8: Specify what you would monitor for a described system and the alert threshold, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Specify what you would monitor and the alert threshold.
bands.11–12: Specify and run monitoring for a real system, and show one drift it caught.

themes.theme: A user who does not know it is a model
themes.description: Disclosure treated as a design requirement of the interface rather than a legal footnote.

bands.K–2: Say why people should always be told when they are talking to a machine.
bands.3–5: Design how a school tool tells users they are talking to a model.
bands.6–8: Design the disclosure for one interface, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design the disclosure for one interface.
bands.11–12: Design and test the disclosure for a real interface with real users, and check they understood it.

themes.theme: Turning it off
themes.description: The conditions for withdrawal, agreed before launch.

bands.K–2: Say when a helper should be switched off, before you start using it.
bands.3–5: Write the conditions under which a school tool would be withdrawn.
bands.6–8: Write the withdrawal criteria for a described system, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the withdrawal criteria for a system, agreed before it launches.
bands.11–12: Write the withdrawal criteria for a real system before launch and get them agreed by the people who could invoke them.

themes.theme: Documenting the system for whoever inherits it
themes.description: What the next team needs and rarely receives.

bands.K–2: Write what the next class would need to know to use a tool you set up.
bands.3–5: Write the notes the next team would need to run a school tool.
bands.6–8: Produce the handover documentation for a described system, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce the handover documentation the next team would need and rarely receives.
bands.11–12: Produce the handover documentation for a real system and have the inheriting team run it from the documentation alone.

themes.theme: What a benchmark measures
themes.description: The gap between the benchmark and the deployment.

bands.K–2: Say why a test with easy questions does not show what a helper does in real life.
bands.3–5: Look at one test a model passed and say what it did not test.
bands.6–8: Identify one benchmark and what it does not test, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one benchmark and what it does not test.
bands.11–12: Identify the benchmarks cited for a system in real use and what each fails to test about that use.

themes.theme: Building your own test set
themes.description: Testing on your cases rather than somebody else’s.

bands.K–2: Make your own list of questions to test a helper on things your class cares about.
bands.3–5: Build a small test set for a real school task instead of using somebody else's.
bands.6–8: Assemble a test set for a real task, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Assemble a test set for a real task from your own cases rather than somebody else's.
bands.11–12: Assemble a test set for a real organisation's task with the people who do it, and run it.

themes.theme: Measuring the failures that matter most
themes.description: Weighting errors by consequence rather than counting them.

bands.K–2: Say which mistakes by a helper would matter most, and count those first.
bands.3–5: Weight a set of model errors by how much harm each would do.
bands.6–8: Weight one error set by consequence, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Weight one error set by consequence rather than by count, and rank the failures.
bands.11–12: Weight a real system's errors by consequence with the people affected, and report the weighted result.

themes.theme: Red-teaming without theatre
themes.description: Adversarial testing that produces findings rather than a report.

bands.K–2: Try to make a helper say something wrong on purpose and write down what worked.
bands.3–5: Try to break a school tool on purpose and record what you found.
bands.6–8: Run one red-team exercise on a described system and record findings, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Run one red-team exercise and record findings.
bands.11–12: Run a red-team exercise on a real system with a scope agreed in advance and deliver findings that were fixed.

themes.theme: Testing with the people affected
themes.description: Evaluation that includes the people the system acts on.

bands.K–2: Ask the people a tool is used on what they think of it.
bands.3–5: Design a test of a school tool that includes the pupils it is used on.
bands.6–8: Design an evaluation that includes the people the system acts on, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design an evaluation that includes them.
bands.11–12: Design and run an evaluation of a real system with the people it acts on, and publish their findings alongside yours.

themes.theme: A result that does not replicate
themes.description: Variance across identical runs, and reporting the spread rather than the best result.

bands.K–2: Ask a helper the same question five times and notice the answers change.
bands.3–5: Run a model test five times and report the range, not the best.
bands.6–8: Run one evaluation five times and report the spread, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Run one evaluation five times and report the spread.
bands.11–12: Run a real evaluation five times, report the spread, and correct a published best-run claim.

themes.theme: Comparing two systems fairly
themes.description: Matched conditions, and the comparisons that are meaningless.

bands.K–2: Compare two helpers with the same questions, not different ones.
bands.3–5: Design a fair test between two tools with the same conditions for both.
bands.6–8: Design a fair comparison between two systems, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a fair comparison between two systems under matched conditions.
bands.11–12: Design and run a fair comparison for a real choice between systems, and report it to the people choosing.

themes.theme: Evaluating for a subgroup
themes.description: Aggregate performance hiding a failure for a specific group.

bands.K–2: Check whether a helper works as well for everyone in the class, not just most.
bands.3–5: Split a test result by group and find one group the tool fails.
bands.6–8: Disaggregate one evaluation by subgroup, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Disaggregate one evaluation by subgroup and report what the aggregate hid.
bands.11–12: Disaggregate a real evaluation, find the group the aggregate hid, and report it.

themes.theme: Publishing an evaluation of somebody’s product
themes.description: Evaluating somebody else’s product accurately, defensibly, and in public.

bands.K–2: Write a fair review of a helper, saying what you tested.
bands.3–5: Write a review of a real tool that its makers could not call unfair.
bands.6–8: Write an evaluation of somebody's product to a standard you would defend, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write one to a standard you would defend.
bands.11–12: Publish an evaluation of a real product to a defensible standard and respond to the maker's reply.

themes.theme: The evaluation you would want run on you
themes.description: Applying your own standard to your own system.

bands.K–2: Test your own project the way you would test someone else's.
bands.3–5: Apply your own test standard to something you built and say the result honestly.
bands.6–8: Apply your own standard to your own system and report the result, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Apply the evaluation you would want run on you to your own system and report the result.
bands.11–12: Apply your standard to a real system you built, publish the result, and act on it.

themes.theme: Where a dataset came from
themes.description: Tracing provenance, and the point at which it becomes untraceable.

bands.6–8: Trace one dataset as far back as it goes and mark where it becomes untraceable, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace one dataset as far back as it goes.
bands.11–12: Trace the datasets behind a real system as far as they go and report where provenance ends, for the people accountable.

themes.theme: Consent that was never given
themes.description: Data collected for one purpose used for another.

bands.3–5: Find one case where data collected for one thing was used for another, and say what was wrong.
bands.6–8: Identify one case of data reused without consent and state the issue, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one case of data collected for one purpose and used for another, and state the issue.
bands.11–12: Identify a real case in a real organisation's data and state the issue to the people who can remedy it.

themes.theme: Licences, and what they actually permit
themes.description: Reading a data licence for what it allows downstream.

bands.K–2: Say what a 'you may use this' label on a picture lets you do and not do.
bands.3–5: Read one data licence and list what it lets somebody do afterwards.
bands.6–8: Read one licence and state the downstream permissions, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read one licence and state the permissions.
bands.11–12: Read the licences of a real system's data and state, for its builders, what each permits and forbids.

themes.theme: Scraping, and the argument about it
themes.description: The case for and against training on scraped material, each stated as its holders would.

bands.3–5: State the case for and against training on scraped material, fairly, as each side would.
bands.6–8: Present both cases on scraping to a standard each side would accept, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Present both to a standard each side would accept.
bands.11–12: Present both cases to a real audience holding both views and have each confirm their case was stated fairly.

themes.theme: The workers who labelled it
themes.description: The annotation labour behind a dataset, and its conditions.

bands.K–2: Say that people label the pictures and words a helper learns from, and ask who they are.
bands.3–5: Describe the people who labelled one dataset and how they were treated.
bands.6–8: Describe the labour behind one dataset and its conditions, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Describe the annotation labour behind one dataset and the conditions it was done under.
bands.11–12: Describe the labour behind a real system's data, with sources, for the people who deploy it.

themes.theme: Personal data inside a training set
themes.description: Recognising it, and what removal would require.

bands.K–2: Say how you might tell whether a dataset has real people's private details in it.
bands.3–5: Check a small dataset for names, addresses and other personal details.
bands.6–8: Assess one dataset for personal data and what removal would require, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Assess one dataset for personal data and state what removal would require.
bands.11–12: Assess a real dataset for personal data, state what removal would require, and start it.

themes.theme: Synthetic data and what it inherits
themes.description: What generated data carries from what generated it.

bands.3–5: Find one thing generated data carries from the data it was made from.
bands.6–8: Identify the inheritance in one case of synthetic data, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify what synthetic data inherits from its source in one real case.
bands.11–12: Identify what synthetic data in a real pipeline inherits from its source and document it for its users.

themes.theme: A dataset withdrawn after publication
themes.description: What happens to models already trained on it.

bands.3–5: Describe what happens to a model already trained on a dataset that is later withdrawn.
bands.6–8: Describe the practical consequences of a dataset withdrawal for models trained on it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Describe the practical consequences of a dataset withdrawal for models already trained on it.
bands.11–12: Describe the practical consequences for a real system of a real withdrawal, and the response the organisation should make.

themes.theme: Documentation a dataset should carry
themes.description: What a datasheet contains and why it is usually absent.

bands.K–2: Write a label for a class dataset: what it is, where it came from, what it is for.
bands.3–5: Write a short datasheet for a school dataset.
bands.6–8: Write a datasheet for one dataset, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a datasheet for one dataset that had none, covering what it contains and how it was made.
bands.11–12: Write the datasheet for a dataset in real use that had none, and get it adopted.

themes.theme: Data you would refuse to use
themes.description: Drawing your own line on data you will not use, and writing it down before it is tested.

bands.3–5: Write your own rule for data you will not use, before anyone asks you to.
bands.6–8: Write your own refusal on data and its reasoning, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write your own refusal and its reasoning.
bands.11–12: Write your refusal, publish it with your reasoning, and hold to it in a real case.

tracks.name: Value, work and who captures it

themes.theme: Who pays and who benefits
themes.description: Tracing the value from a deployed system to the parties involved.

bands.3–5: Map who pays and who benefits from one school system.
bands.6–8: Map the flow of value for one described deployment, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map who pays and who benefits across one real deployment.
bands.11–12: Map the value flow for a real deployment and present it to the parties who did not know their place in it.

themes.theme: A task automated and a wage removed

bands.6–8: Do the arithmetic for one real role when a task is automated, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Do the wage arithmetic for one real role when part of it is automated.
bands.11–12: Do the arithmetic for a real role with the person who holds it, and present it to the people deciding.

bands.6–8: Trace one documented case of productivity gains to where they landed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace one documented case of productivity gains to wages, prices or margins.
bands.11–12: Trace a real case in a real sector to wages, prices or margins, and publish the finding.

themes.theme: The cost that moved rather than vanished

bands.3–5: Find one cost that a system moved onto customers or the public instead of removing.
bands.6–8: Identify one cost that moved onto users or the public rather than disappearing, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one cost that moved onto users or the public rather than disappearing.
bands.11–12: Identify the moved costs of a real deployment and add them to its business case.

themes.theme: Infrastructure and who owns it

bands.3–5: Map who owns one layer of the computing behind a system.
bands.6–8: Map the ownership in one layer of the stack, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map the ownership in one layer of the stack.
bands.11–12: Map the ownership behind a real deployment across the stack and present the dependencies to the organisation.

themes.theme: Small organisations and access

bands.3–5: Work out what one capability would cost a small organisation.
bands.6–8: Cost one capability for a small organisation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Cost one capability for a small organisation.
bands.11–12: Cost a capability for a real small organisation and advise them honestly on whether it is available to them.

themes.theme: A market with three suppliers

bands.3–5: Describe what competition looks like when only a few companies can afford to build.
bands.6–8: Describe the dynamics in one market with few suppliers, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Describe the dynamics in one such market.
bands.11–12: Describe the dynamics of a real concentrated market for the people who buy from it.

themes.theme: Public procurement of these systems

bands.3–5: Write what a public body should require before buying a system.
bands.6–8: Write the requirements a public body should insist on, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the requirements you would insist on.
bands.11–12: Write the requirements for a real public procurement and get them into the tender.

themes.theme: Taxation, and where the value is booked

bands.6–8: Trace one company's booked profit against where the work was done, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace one company's booked profit against where the work was actually done.
bands.11–12: Trace a real company's booked profit against where its work happened and present the gap to a body that could act.

themes.theme: An alternative ownership model

bands.3–5: Argue for one different way to own a system, such as a cooperative.
bands.6–8: Argue one alternative ownership model concretely, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Argue one alternative ownership model concretely, including what it would require.
bands.11–12: Argue an alternative ownership model for a real system to the people who could adopt it, with what it would require.

themes.theme: Deciding what you will not do

bands.3–5: Write your own line for using models and one situation that would test it.
bands.6–8: Write your own line and one case that would test it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write your own line and one case that would test it.
bands.11–12: Write your line, hold it in a real case that tested it, and record what it cost.

themes.theme: Working on something you have doubts about

bands.6–8: Prepare a conversation voicing a concern about work you have doubts about, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Prepare a conversation that voices a concern about work you have doubts about, usefully.
bands.11–12: Have the real conversation about real work you have doubts about, and record what changed.

bands.3–5: Plan and follow a week of practising a skill you usually delegate.
bands.6–8: Design a practice schedule for a delegated skill and run it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design a practice schedule for a skill you have delegated, and run it.
bands.11–12: Design and run a practice schedule for a term, and measure whether the judgement held.

themes.theme: Reading outside the field

bands.6–8: Read one outside source and state what it changed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read one outside source and state what it changed.
bands.11–12: Read outside sources for a term, state what each changed, and bring one into your real work.

themes.theme: Explaining your work to somebody it affects

bands.3–5: Explain a school project to somebody it affects and write down their response.
bands.6–8: Explain your work to somebody it affects and record their response, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain your work to somebody it affects, and record their response.
bands.11–12: Explain real work to real people it affects, record their responses, and change the work where warranted.

themes.theme: Being wrong publicly

bands.3–5: Write a correction of something you argued before, for everyone to see.
bands.6–8: Write a correction of a real past position, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a correction of a real past position.
bands.11–12: Publish a correction of a real position you argued for, and record what it cost and bought.

themes.theme: The colleague who disagrees with you

bands.3–5: Describe how you would keep working with a classmate you truly disagree with.
bands.6–8: Describe how you would hold a working relationship across a genuine disagreement, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Describe how you would hold a working relationship across a genuine disagreement.
bands.11–12: Hold a real working relationship across a real disagreement, and write what it required.

themes.theme: Hype, and your own contribution to it

bands.3–5: Check three things you said about a technology for exaggeration.
bands.6–8: Audit three of your own claims about technology for overstatement, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Audit three of your own claims about technology for overstatement.
bands.11–12: Audit your public claims over a year, correct the overstatements, and publish the audit.

themes.theme: What you would want your work judged on

bands.3–5: Write the standard you want your work judged by, in advance.
bands.6–8: Write the standard you would want your own work judged against, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the standard you would want your own work judged against.

bands.9–10: Write the advice you would give somebody starting, specific enough to act on, for a real reader.
